1.grade_fit_note: Key copies the passage's next-season sentence almost word for word; the three distractors describe equipment and settings the passage never mentions.
1.note: Verbatim retrieval. A student who finds the last paragraph matches 'bright and dark nights alike' directly. Distractors keep the 'X and Y alike' frame, so the shape gives nothing away, but none of them can be found in the text.

2.grade_fit_note: Crickets are the only visitor the passage names; geckos, bats and hawkmoths never appear.
2.note: Explaining why it matters takes one step (moonlight and predators), but the distractors introduce animals that are not in the passage, so recognising the cricket settles it without any reasoning.

3.grade_fit_note: The key is a close paraphrase of the paragraph 2 sentence; wind, rain and temperature are never mentioned.
3.note: Literal recall. The distractors' precise numbers make them look careful, but nothing in the text backs them.

4.grade_fit_note: Weakening an explanation is real grade 8 work (RI.8.8), but three options are about animals her explanation never involves.
4.free_elimination: A, B and C name hawkmoths, geckos and nectar bats, which are absent from the passage; any student who knows the cricket is the visitor removes them without evaluating anything.
4.note: The best concept in the set, spoiled by its distractors: to make students actually evaluate the evidence, the wrong options would have to concern crickets, the owl or moonlight.

5.grade_fit_note: The passage explicitly denies B (the voter roll was not enlarged), C (no covenant of repair) and D (surveyors found every scheme fit).
5.note: The inference that Marrable was the largest employer is mild. Each distractor is denied by its own sentence in paragraph 2, so the item tests elimination by lookup. The archaic diction makes it harder to read, not harder to answer.

6.grade_fit_note: The passage says the diary's worth 'is that it exposes an omission in the official record'; that is the key verbatim.
6.note: Each distractor is negated in so many words in paragraph 4. A, C and D do match passage wording, so they may catch students who match words without reading the negation, but not a grade 8 reader.

7.grade_fit_note: 'The board acted carelessly' is stated outright, and admiration, detachment and irony/self-interest are each explicitly denied.
7.note: An attitude question that needs no inference about tone. The passage announces its attitude and lists the rejected alternatives.

8.grade_fit_note: Stated in paragraph 1. The only friction is the archaic 'went down on the second reading' applied to the canal.
8.note: A is the one live lure: the canal is named right next to the resolution, and a weak reader may not see that 'went down' means it was rejected.

9.grade_fit_note: Only one option names the railway; once the scheme is known, the 'because' clause never needs to be read.
9.free_elimination: B, C and D name schemes the passage says were rejected; item 8 on the same passage establishes the railway, so the noun alone settles it.
9.note: Labelled main idea, but it works as a recall item. The key also leaves out the tolls, the diary and the author's verdict, so as a main idea it is thin. Options are noun-phrase fragments, not statements.

10.grade_fit_note: The passage defines 'check' in the next clause and then rules out the other three senses by name.
10.note: The distractors are genuine senses of 'check' (a restraint, a crack, a cheque) and would be good in a context-clue item, but the text itself says 'She did not mean' each one.

11.grade_fit_note: Her one refusal is stated directly: no hand she had not trained herself on the flat.
11.note: A, C and D are each contradicted by the same sentence (largest orders, lifted whenever ready, worked the far flat like any other).

12.grade_fit_note: Purpose stated verbatim ('so that the memory of him would stay in plain view'); boundary, tide signal and shoal warning denied by name.
12.note: Labelled author's purpose/structure, but it is literal recall. Without the denial sentence, B and C would be strong literal-minded lures.

13.grade_fit_note: Only B names the narrator's real job (item 14), and only B's lesson matches the aunt's stated refusal.
13.free_elimination: A, C and D begin with activities the passage says the narrator did not do (or that are not his job); knowing the tally-book fact from item 14 settles it.
13.note: As a main idea the key is shaky: the narrator says he thought her wrong about trained hands, so 'a lesson in working with trained hands' misstates what he took away. It is correct only by elimination.

14.grade_fit_note: Stated in paragraph 1; the other three are listed in the next sentence as tasks the aunt kept for herself.
14.note: The distractors are real lexical lures because they are quoted from the passage, so a skimmer could grab one. A grade 8 reader will not.

15.grade_fit_note: 'I respected her hands and thought her wrong about the flat', followed by explicit denials of comic, cool-observer and unreserved regard.
15.note: Mapping 'never struck me as comic' to C and 'never the unreserved kind' to B takes a small paraphrase step. The stem calls the narrator 'his', but the passage never gives the narrator's gender.

16.grade_fit_note: A matches a sentence verbatim and B, C and D are each explicitly denied, so elimination gives A. A careful reader, though, hits a contradiction.
16.note: FLAW: the paragraph says 'The finding is proved and of small consequence', then 'I will not say flatly that the finding is proved' and refuses 'likely' too, so the writer's actual position is incoherent. A wins only as the least-contradicted option, and a close reader may freeze or protest.

17.grade_fit_note: 'The counts are for the school move' is stated, and each rival is dismissed in its own sentence.
17.note: Literal retrieval. The fare cut (A) is the only distractor with some real-world pull.

18.grade_fit_note: The quoted phrase in the stem ('marks the county boundary') already contains the answer.
18.free_elimination: B and C can be removed from the stem's own quotation, since a line that marks a county boundary is neither a queue nor a row of print; the passage also denies D.
18.note: There is no vocabulary-in-context demand: the key restates the quoted phrase. Paragraph 3 then spends four sentences ruling out the other senses.

19.grade_fit_note: The four options are the four candidate causes, and the passage plainly backs the school move.
19.note: It overlaps with item 17 so much that answering one answers the other. As a main-idea item it is acceptable.

20.grade_fit_note: 'moving the high school back would drop the riders away' is stated, and the other three are each said to have been tried with nobody stopping riding.
20.note: The stem says 'suggests', but the answer is stated outright. It also duplicates the school-move fact tested in items 17 and 19.

21.grade_fit_note: 'What the driver's log supplies is a weather note' is stated, and count, time and name are each denied.
21.note: Labelled purpose/structure, but the options are content, not functions, so no analysis of purpose is involved. The log's role in the argument is also unclear, so a real function question could not be asked anyway.

22.grade_fit_note: 'The answer was the promise' is stated, and the other three are each disproved in the next sentences.
22.note: Literal retrieval, set up in paragraph 1 as a four-way choice and answered in paragraph 2 with the same four options.

23.grade_fit_note: Stated verbatim; each distractor is said to have happened 'that June' while 'the boat stayed in the shed'.
23.note: The stem says 'suggests', but the key is a quoted sentence. It also repeats item 22's fact.

24.grade_fit_note: The next words define the hold as 'a grip worn smooth by two hands', and the other senses are denied in the following sentences.
24.free_elimination: B (an opinion) can be removed from the stem's quotation, since a hold 'on the gunwale' is physical.
24.note: D has some real pull because of a ship's 'hold'. Otherwise the passage's denial sentences answer the item.

25.grade_fit_note: 'What the letter on the shed door supplies is a name' is stated, and date, sum and instruction are each denied.
25.note: The stem says 'pinned inside the shed door' but the passage says 'on the shed door', a small mismatch. As in item 21, the options are content, not functions.

26.grade_fit_note: Answering it requires the same fact as item 22.
26.note: 'Chiefly concerned with' is defensible, but the item is a reworded version of item 22. Its three distractors are explicitly disproved.

27.grade_fit_note: 'What I felt for him then was anger', followed by explicit denials of pity, relief and impatience.
27.note: There is no inference about feeling: the narrator names it and rules out the rest. The stem calls the narrator 'her', but the passage never gives the narrator's gender.

28.grade_fit_note: Stated directly; the passage then says 'Nothing else about the four differed: the same water...', which kills A and D.
28.note: Literal detail. The distractors are realistic experimental variables but appear nowhere in the text.

29.grade_fit_note: Only D describes something in the untreated-pools paragraph; A, B and C report results that are not in the passage.
29.note: C borrows the passage's 'thirteen', which may lure a skimmer, and B contradicts the fact that pool D took no animals for eight nights. The stem points to the right paragraph, so locating the key is easy.

30.grade_fit_note: Purpose stated verbatim: 'to learn whether the animals approached the pools directly or by searching.'
30.note: B is a sensible scientific question and the only distractor with any pull. A ('borrowed scent') and D (shade, old basins) refer to nothing in the passage.

31.grade_fit_note: A genuine multiple-meaning word with a clear but not stated context clue ('drew the path... on a sheet of waxed paper'), suitable for L.6-8.4a.
31.note: The only item in the set where the distractors are real competing senses not ruled out by the text. D ('attracted') is reinforced by the experiment's theme of pools drawing animals.
